intro: Read the deck for the evidence and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains why a slide matters, how to hold it in memory and where people slip. Work the examples in pencil, answer the recall questions without looking, and write your own notes in the margins.

sections.title: Why Inequality Matters
sections.big_idea: Inequality is a moral concern with measurable costs. **Name which kind** you mean before you argue about whether it matters.
in_plain_words: The word inequality covers several different things. Outcome inequality is the unequal result at a moment in time, and opportunity inequality is the unequal chances on the way there. Vertical inequality ranks individuals, while horizontal inequality compares groups such as castes and regions. Poverty is a separate idea again: a fixed line below which people fall.

The evidence for caring runs through five channels: growth, poverty reduction, health, democracy and mobility. Piketty's r > g adds a structural reason for worry, since wealth concentrates whenever capital earns more than the economy grows. **Both the moral case and the empirical case** point the same way, though people hold different theories of justice.

diagram.caption: the five channels through which inequality does damage

key_terms.meaning: Unequal income, wealth or wellbeing at a point in time.
Unequal chances to achieve outcomes.
Gaps between groups such as castes, religions and regions.
The claim that inequality rises then falls with development.
Capital returns above growth make wealth inequality rise.
Rawls: make the worst-off person as well off as possible.

worked_example.title: Poverty fell, inequality rose
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's two India facts for 1991 to 2012 and 1981 to 2022.
steps: Absolute poverty fell from roughly 45% to 22%.
The fall in points is 45 − 22 = 23.
The top 1% income share went from 6% to 22.6%.
The rise in points is 22.6 − 6 = 16.6.
Both are true at once, so one headline cannot stand for the other.
worked_example.answer: Poverty fell by 23 points while the top 1% share rose by 16.6 points. Report them separately.

mistakes: Treating a fall in poverty as proof that inequality fell. The deck shows the two moving in opposite directions in India.
Assuming growth will cure inequality by itself. The Kuznets prediction has largely been rejected by post-1980 data.
Using one theory of justice without saying so. Most policy arguments hide an ethical framework underneath.
Judging India's Gini from consumption data alone. It understates income and wealth inequality.

recall.q: What is the difference between outcome and opportunity inequality?
recall.a: Outcome inequality is the unequal result at a point in time. Opportunity inequality is the unequal chances to achieve results.

recall.q: Who coined horizontal inequality, and what does it compare?
recall.a: Frances Stewart. It compares culturally defined groups such as castes, communities, genders and regions.

recall.q: Name the five channels through which inequality does damage.
recall.a: Growth, poverty reduction, health and wellbeing, democracy, and social mobility.

recall.q: What does r > g predict?
recall.a: When the return on capital exceeds economic growth, wealth inequality tends to rise.

recall.q: Which finding challenges trickle-down?
recall.a: Hope and Limberg (2020): across 18 OECD countries over 50 years, top tax cuts raised inequality with no measurable effect on growth or jobs.

sections.title: Measuring Inequality
sections.big_idea: No single number tells the story. **Choose the measure that fits the decision**, and state why you chose it.
in_plain_words: The Gini coefficient summarises a whole distribution between 0 (everyone equal) and 1 (one person has everything). It is easy to quote but blind to where in the distribution a change happens. Income shares, the Palma ratio and the Theil index each answer a narrower question, and the MPI and IHDI look beyond money to health, education and living standards.

For India the choice of data matters as much as the choice of measure. HCES consumption data gives a Gini of about 0.35, tax records and WID.world show far more concentration at the top, and PLFS misses capital income. **Surveys miss the very rich**, so the honest position is that India's true inequality is higher than official statistics suggest.

diagram.note: a ratio of the two extremes, so it moves when the top or bottom moves

key_terms.meaning: Summary measure from 0 to 1, drawn from the Lorenz curve.
Plots cumulative income share against cumulative population share.
Top 10% income share divided by the bottom 40% share.
Entropy-based measure split into within-group and between-group parts.
Multidimensional Poverty Index: overlapping deprivations in health, education, living standards.
HDI discounted for inequality in each dimension.

worked_example.title: Work out a Palma ratio
worked_example.setup: First use the deck's India figures, then an illustrative district.
steps: The deck uses a top 10% share of 57 and a bottom 50% share of 15.
57 ÷ 15 = 3.8, a ratio of the top 10% to the bottom 50%.
The bottom 40% hold less than the bottom 50%, so India's Palma ratio is above 3.8. In an illustrative district the top 10% hold 40 and the bottom 40% hold 20.
The district's top group earns twice the bottom group's total, a smaller gap than India.
worked_example.answer: India's Palma ratio is above 3.8 on the deck's figures, and the illustrative district is 2.

mistakes: Quoting the consumption Gini as if it were the income Gini. The deck puts the gap at 0.10 to 0.15 points.
Assuming two societies with the same Gini have the same distribution. Different shapes can share one Gini.
Using Theil without asking what the decomposition is for. It tells you whether to target places or people.
Reading MPI as the same as income poverty. Households can be above the income line and still MPI poor.

recall.q: What are the limits of the Gini?
recall.a: Different distributions can share a Gini, it is insensitive to transfers at the top or bottom, it is hard to compare across data quality, and India's consumption Gini understates income inequality.

recall.q: How is the Palma ratio defined?
recall.a: The top 10% income share divided by the bottom 40% income share.

recall.q: When would you use the Theil decomposition?
recall.a: To see whether inequality is mostly between regions or within them, which guides geographic against community-level targeting.

recall.q: What is the MPI threshold for a poor household?
recall.a: Deprived in at least 33% of weighted indicators, across 10 indicators.

recall.q: Why do surveys understate top incomes?
recall.a: The rich underreport or refuse surveys, so household surveys miss the top of the distribution.

sections.title: Income vs Wealth Inequality
sections.big_idea: Income is a flow and wealth is a stock. **Wealth compounds**, so it concentrates faster and is harder to see.
in_plain_words: Most poor households live on labour income, while the wealthy own assets that throw off income automatically: land, property, shares and business stakes. If the return on capital runs above growth, as the deck says Indian equities did against GDP, ownership pulls ahead of work. That is why the labour share of income has been falling.

Wealth is also harder to see. It hides in trusts, shell companies and benami property, and India has no wealth registry. Inheritance carries it across generations, and policy has removed the main correctives: estate duty in 1985 and wealth tax in 2015. **Land and gender** add two more layers, since land is concentrated and women own about 14% of it.

left.title: Income (a flow)
items: Visible in tax returns and surveys
Poor households rely on labour income

right.title: Wealth (a stock)
items: Hidden in trusts and benami holdings
Compounds and passes on by inheritance

key_terms.meaning: What you earn over a period, such as wages or dividends.
What you have accumulated, such as land or shares.
The share of national income going to workers.
Hindu Undivided Family: a joint family taxed as a separate unit.
Property held under a proxy name.
Finance growing in weight, with returns to ownership rising.

worked_example.title: Flow or stock?
worked_example.setup: Sort six items, then check the gap between returns and growth.
steps: A monthly salary and a dividend payment are flows.
A plot of land and a block of shares are stocks.
Rent received is a flow, and the flat that earns it is a stock.
The deck gives equity returns of 15 to 18% and GDP growth of 6 to 7%.
The narrowest gap is 15 − 7 = 8 points, and the widest is 18 − 6 = 12 points.
worked_example.answer: Equities beat growth by 8 to 12 points a year, so owners of financial assets pull ahead.

mistakes: Taxing income and expecting wealth concentration to ease. The deck says wealth is where the power sits.
Treating payments access as wealth building. UPI helps transactions but not savings or investment.
Reading the failed wealth tax as proof that wealth taxes cannot work. Critics call it a design failure.
Overlooking women's land ownership. It is a strong predictor of agency and of lower domestic violence.

recall.q: Why is wealth inequality harder to measure than income inequality?
recall.a: Wealth hides in shell companies, benami property, foreign accounts and trusts, and India has no wealth registry or wealth tax.

recall.q: What is the land Gini and what does it show?
recall.a: About 0.74 (NSSO 2012-13), one of the most unequal land distributions in Asia.

recall.q: When were India's estate duty and wealth tax abolished?
recall.a: Estate duty in 1985 and wealth tax in 2015.

recall.q: What share of land do women own?
recall.a: About 14%, despite being 50% of the population.

recall.q: What does the HUF do for wealthy families?
recall.a: It lets family wealth be held collectively and taxed separately, a tax arbitrage the deck calls under-examined.

sections.title: Global Trends in Inequality
sections.big_idea: Between countries, inequality fell. Inside countries, it rose. **COVID, AI and climate** now push on the same fault lines.
in_plain_words: Milanovic's elephant curve shows who gained between 1988 and 2008. Asian workers and the global top 1% did well, while rich-country working and middle classes stagnated. Between-country inequality fell as China and India grew faster than rich nations, yet within-country inequality rose in most major economies.

Since then three forces have arrived. COVID raised billionaire wealth and pushed 97M people into extreme poverty. Technology and AI could hollow out jobs before India builds a manufacturing base. Climate change falls hardest on the rural poor, who emitted least. **SDG 10** sets the target of faster income growth for the bottom 40%, but nothing about it is automatic.

diagram.caption: the global story in five dates

key_terms.meaning: Milanovic's chart of global income gains by percentile, 1988 to 2008.
Top incomes recover fast while the bottom stagnates.
China's household registration system tying people to place.
Skill-biased technological change favouring skilled work.
The goal to reduce inequality within and among countries.
The OECD/G20 15% global minimum corporate tax.

worked_example.title: Test Target 10.1
worked_example.setup: Target 10.1 asks for bottom 40% income growth above the national average. These growth rates are illustrative.
steps: National income grows 6% a year in a country.
The bottom 40% grow 5% a year.
The shortfall is 6 − 5 = 1 point a year.
The target is therefore missed, even though the bottom is gaining in absolute terms.
worked_example.answer: The target needs bottom 40% growth above 6%, so 5% misses it by 1 point.

mistakes: Reading falling global inequality as good news for every group. The Western middle classes stagnated.
Assuming growth alone delivers SDG 10. The deck says all the targets need active policy choice.
Forgetting that carbon inequality mirrors income inequality. The richest 1% emit more than the bottom 50% combined.
Treating technology as destiny. The slide says direction depends on policy choices.

recall.q: Who gained and who lost on the elephant curve?
recall.a: The global middle (Asian workers) and top 1% gained. The 75th to 85th percentile, rich-country working and middle classes, gained least.

recall.q: What did billionaire wealth do during COVID?
recall.a: The ten richest men's wealth rose from $700 billion to $1.5 trillion in two years.

recall.q: What was China's Gini peak and what lifted it?
recall.a: About 0.49 around 2008, after rising from about 0.28 in 1981, during growth that lifted 800M out of poverty.

recall.q: What is Target 10.1?
recall.a: Income growth of the bottom 40% at a rate higher than the national average.

recall.q: Why is climate policy design an inequality issue?
recall.a: Green taxes can be regressive and renewable land acquisition can displace communities unless distribution is planned.

sections.title: India's Inequality Story
sections.big_idea: Growth after 1991 cut poverty and concentrated income. **Informality, land and regions** explain why the structure holds.
in_plain_words: India's pattern has a clear arc. Colonial rule left high asset inequality and weak institutions. The planned economy then compressed top incomes, with the top 1% share falling to about 6% by 1980. After 1991, a skill premium and a capital income boom took that share to 22.6% in 2022.

Beneath the arc sit structures that do not change quickly. About 90% of workers are informal and earn a fraction of formal pay. Urban consumption runs 1.7 times rural, and regions are diverging. **Billionaire wealth** rose from 9 in 2000 to 205 in 2025. Data caution is part of the story, because HCES and WID.world measure different things.

key_terms.meaning: The pre-1991 system of industrial licensing.
The extra pay for educated, skilled work.
Work without job security, social protection or labour rights.
Household Consumption Expenditure Survey, the official consumption data.
Wealth built through political connections in regulated sectors.
Periodic Labour Force Survey, annual labour market data.

worked_example.title: How far did the top 1% move?
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's top 1% income shares for 1981 and 2022, then the rural-urban ratio.
steps: The share was 6% in 1981 and 22.6% in 2022.
The ratio is 22.6 ÷ 6 = 3.8.
So the top 1% share is about 3.8 times its 1981 level.
For consumption, the urban-rural ratio is 1.7, meaning urban households consume about 70% more.
worked_example.answer: The top 1% share is about 3.8 times higher than in 1981, while urban consumption is 1.7 times rural.

mistakes: Using one data source for every question. The deck assigns HCES to poverty, WID.world to the top, MPI to deprivation.
Calling India's growth a failure because inequality rose. Poverty also fell sharply.
Treating gig work as formal. The deck notes that platform work is informal by default.
Taking national averages as the whole picture. Goa and Bihar sit at opposite ends of regional income.

recall.q: What happened to the top 1% income share between 1981 and 2022?
recall.a: It rose from 6% to 22.6%.

recall.q: What share of India's workforce is informal, and what is the formal wage premium?
recall.a: About 90% informal, with a formal premium of 2 to 3 times.

recall.q: Why is HCES 2022-23 not directly comparable with 2011-12?
recall.a: Methods changed, including imputed rent, and surveys still miss top incomes.

recall.q: How many USD billionaires did India have in 2000, 2010 and 2025?
What are the median monthly wages for casual and regular workers?
recall.a: About Rs 11,000 and about Rs 25,000 (PLFS 2022-23).

sections.title: Caste, Gender & Region
sections.big_idea: Horizontal inequality sorts people by identity. **Disaggregate by caste, gender and religion together**, because disadvantages compound.
in_plain_words: Caste is the most important horizontal axis. SC and ST poverty rates run two to three times those of upper castes, occupations remain segregated and audit studies show lower callbacks for Dalit names. Reservations created a public-sector middle class but reach only the formal 10% of the workforce.

Gender, religion and disability add further axes. Women's labour force participation is low and unpaid care absorbs hours. Muslims, per the Sachar Committee, were found comparable to or worse off than Scheduled Castes on several measures. People with disabilities face higher costs and lower participation. **Intersections** are where outcomes are worst: Dalit women and Adivasi girls.

key_terms.meaning: Crenshaw's term for overlapping, compounding disadvantage.
Quotas in jobs, education and legislatures.
The 2019 10% reservation for economically weaker sections.
Female labour force participation rate.
Disability rights law listing 21 categories.
Matched applications testing discrimination in hiring.

worked_example.title: Bound the upper-caste rate
worked_example.setup: The deck gives an SC poverty rate of 27%, two to three times the upper-caste rate.
steps: If the SC rate is three times the upper-caste rate, divide by 3.
If it is two times, divide by 2.
So the implied upper-caste rate lies between 9% and 13.5%.
worked_example.answer: The implied upper-caste poverty rate is about 9% to 13.5%.

mistakes: Reporting 'women' or 'Dalits' as one group. Averages hide the Dalit woman or Adivasi girl who is falling behind.
Treating reservation as a full answer. It reaches the formal 10% and favours the better-educated.
Reading low female participation as a pure choice. The deck lists norms, safety, income effects and stigma.
Retrofitting accessibility. Universal design from the start costs less and excludes fewer people.

recall.q: What are the central reservation percentages?
recall.a: 15% SC, 7.5% ST, 27% OBC and 10% EWS.

recall.q: What did the Sachar Committee find?
recall.a: Muslims, 14% of the population, were comparable to or in some ways worse off than Scheduled Castes.

recall.q: How many minutes a day do women spend on unpaid domestic work, per the Time Use Survey 2019?
recall.a: 299 minutes, against 97 for men.

recall.q: What does the RPWD Act 2016 reserve in government employment?
recall.a: 4% of posts, with 5% in higher education.

recall.q: Why disaggregate by caste and gender together?
recall.a: Programmes can show overall progress while the most marginalised subgroup falls behind.

sections.title: Health and Education Inequality
sections.big_idea: Health and learning gaps follow income, caste and state. **Kerala against UP** shows that policy choices set the outcome.
in_plain_words: India has near-universal school enrolment, but about 55% of rural Grade 5 children cannot read a Grade 2 text. Two school tracks, private and government, pass birth circumstances into the labour market. On health, stunting, anaemia and mortality are highest among the poorest, SC and ST households and the states with weak systems.

Cost and access compound the gap. Out-of-pocket spending is regressive, 55M people were pushed into poverty in one year, and PM-JAY covers only hospitalisation. The digital divide added a new layer when COVID forced learning online. **Food surplus coexists with hunger** because access limits who eats, whatever the harvest.

key_terms.meaning: National Family Health Survey, the main source of health inequality data.
Annual Status of Education Report, measuring learning levels.
Chronic undernutrition in children under 5.
Health costs paid directly by households.
Ayushman Bharat hospitalisation insurance.
Jan Dhan, Aadhaar and Mobile delivery infrastructure.

worked_example.title: Size the Kerala gap
worked_example.setup: Compare under-5 mortality using the deck's table, with the lower UP/Bihar figure.
steps: Kerala has 7 deaths per 1000 live births.
The lower UP/Bihar figure is 55.
The ratio is 55 ÷ 7 = 7.9.
The upper figure of 65 gives 65 ÷ 7 = 9.3.
Variation within one country is therefore close to 8 to 9 times.
worked_example.answer: Under-5 mortality in UP and Bihar is about 8 to 9 times Kerala's.

mistakes: Using enrolment as a progress metric. The deck says learning levels are the right measure.
Comparing NFHS-5 and NFHS-6 figures without labelling them. Stunting is 35.5% in one and 29.3% in the other.
Treating the outpatient gap as minor. About 60% of health spending is outpatient and PM-JAY does not cover it.
Assuming digital delivery includes everyone. Authentication failures have removed some vulnerable people from rolls.

recall.q: What share of rural Grade 5 children cannot read a Grade 2 text?
recall.a: About 55% (ASER 2024).

recall.q: What was Kerala's route to better health?
recall.a: High female literacy, a strong public system, land reform and high social capital.

recall.q: What is PM-JAY's coverage and gap?
recall.a: Rs 5 lakh a year for 55 crore beneficiaries, but hospitalisation only.

recall.q: What is the out-of-pocket share of health spending in 2021-22?
What is India's Global Hunger Index rank, and why is it a paradox?
recall.a: 111th in 2023, despite food grain surpluses in government warehouses.

sections.title: Intergenerational Mobility
sections.big_idea: Mobility is the long-run test of inequality. **High inequality and low mobility reinforce each other**, unless policy breaks the loop.
in_plain_words: Intergenerational mobility asks how far children's outcomes depend on their parents'. Corak's Great Gatsby Curve shows that unequal countries tend to be less mobile, and India sits at the unequal, immobile end. Caste is the strongest predictor of occupational persistence, working through discrimination and network exclusion.

Four channels offer a way out, each with limits. Education is filtered by school quality. Migration brings income but loses social protection. Reservation creates a first-mover advantage. Networks pass on jobs and credit. **Policy responds**: early childhood, school quality, portable protection and anti-discrimination enforcement all raise mobility.

key_terms.meaning: Intergenerational income elasticity: link between parents' and children's incomes.
Higher inequality goes with lower mobility across countries.
Sub-caste ties carrying information, credit and patronage.
Networks, reciprocity and trust that open access.
Benefits that move with the worker.
Gains for the family of the first person in formal employment.

worked_example.title: Match the policy to the barrier
worked_example.setup: Pair each barrier with the deck's best-fit policy.
steps: A migrant loses a ration card on moving: portable social protection.
Teacher absence and weak pedagogy: government school quality reform.
A first 1000 days with poor nutrition: early childhood investment.
Lower callbacks for Dalit names: anti-discrimination enforcement.
worked_example.answer: Portability, school reform, early childhood investment and enforcement.

mistakes: Treating mobility as fixed by culture. The slides say it responds to policy.
Counting education access as equal opportunity. Quality inequality turns access into reinforcement.
Calling migration a mobility success without asking about protection. Many moves are circular and precarious.
Ignoring networks. Jati networks carry jobs and credit that marginalised groups lack.

recall.q: What does the Great Gatsby Curve show?
recall.a: Higher inequality is associated with lower intergenerational mobility across countries.

recall.q: Why is mothers' education important?
recall.a: It has the largest effect on a child's educational attainment.

recall.q: What did the March 2020 lockdown reveal about migrants?
recall.a: No portable access to PDS rations, MGNREGS work or social insurance.

recall.q: What was Ambedkar's description of caste?
recall.a: A system of graded inequality, with each caste superior to some and inferior to others.

recall.q: Which scheme is an example of portability?
recall.a: One Nation One Ration Card, still incompletely implemented.

sections.title: Causes of Inequality
sections.big_idea: Inequality has several interacting causes. **No single driver and no single fix** explains or cures it.
in_plain_words: Technology comes first. SBTC rewards skills and replaces routine work, and India's IT boom created a skill premium. Globalisation lifted average incomes but its gains went to the educated and to capital owners. Financialisation then turned market booms into wealth for existing owners in equities, real estate and private equity.

Policy, discrimination and history complete the picture. Falling top tax rates, untaxed inheritance and regressive subsidy incidence all shaped outcomes. Discrimination operates now in hiring, housing and credit. The colonial legacy shaped assets and institutions. **History is not self-correcting**, so active redistribution is needed alongside growth.

key_terms.meaning: Technology that complements skilled work and replaces routine tasks.
Trade opening benefits a country's abundant factor.
1793 Bengal arrangement creating hereditary zamindars.
Who actually receives a subsidy's benefit.
Direct Benefit Transfer: cash in place of in-kind subsidy.
Early conditions shaping later outcomes.

worked_example.title: Match cause to response
worked_example.setup: The deck says causal mechanisms guide programme design. Pair each cause with a response.
steps: Skill-biased technology: education and training for the affected workers.
Present-day discrimination: anti-discrimination measures alongside asset building.
Path dependency from history: active redistribution alongside growth.
Regressive subsidies or taxes: a redesigned tax or transfer, with attention to access.
worked_example.answer: Training, anti-discrimination measures, redistribution and tax or transfer redesign.

mistakes: Blaming one cause. The slide lists six and says they interact.
Expecting globalisation to favour labour in India. Exports tilted to skilled services.
Treating discrimination as history only. Audit studies show present-day callback gaps.
Assuming DBT includes everyone. People without accounts or phones face access challenges.

recall.q: How did India's trade structure violate the textbook prediction?
recall.a: Labour-abundant India exported skill-intensive services, so benefits went to skilled workers and left unskilled labour behind.

recall.q: What did the Banerjee et al. audit study find?
recall.a: No discrimination in software jobs but lower callbacks for OBC applicants in call centre jobs.

recall.q: What happened to India's share of world manufacturing?
recall.a: It fell from roughly 25% in 1750 to 2% in 1900 (Bairoch).

recall.q: What share of equity market value do the top 10% of investors hold?
recall.a: Over 90%, so equity booms flow almost entirely to the already wealthy.

recall.q: Why did colonial rule make caste more rigid?
recall.a: Census operations, separate electorates and legal classification fixed categories and used caste as an administrative unit.

sections.title: Policy Responses
sections.big_idea: The interventions that reduce inequality are well understood. **The gap is political**, because concentrated wealth resists redistribution.
in_plain_words: This section covers six instruments. Progressive taxation is the core tool, but India's top rate fell and capital gains are taxed lightly. Social protection exists at scale through PDS, MGNREGS, PM-KISAN, PM-JAY and PM-AWAS, with coverage gaps for urban informal, migrant and gig workers. MGNREGS has strong evidence of impact.

The rest are contested. Reservations have measurable benefits within the formal sector and clear limits. Land reform is partial but existing laws could still do more. UBI has pilots and a 2016-17 proposal but no national scheme. **What is missing** is a wealth and inheritance framework, private sector anti-discrimination enforcement, portability, an urban guarantee and land reform enforcement.

key_terms.meaning: A tax whose rate rises with income or wealth.
A legitimate beneficiary denied access.
Rural employment guarantee scheme.
10% reservation for economically weaker sections from 2019.
Unconditional cash transfer to every citizen.
Tax revenue as a share of GDP; about 18 to 19% in India.

worked_example.title: Size an illustrative UBI
worked_example.setup: The 2016-17 Survey proposed Rs 7,620 per person per year to 75% of the population. Apply it to an illustrative village of 1,000 people.
steps: Recipients are 1,000 × 75 ÷ 100 = 750.
Annual payout is 750 × 7,620 = 5,715,000.
The village figure scales up to a national bill, which the deck puts at 5 to 7% of GDP.
The cost is why critics call UBI prohibitive without subsidy rationalisation.
worked_example.answer: The village would receive Rs 5,715,000 a year.

mistakes: Quoting 100 days for MGNREGS without the correction. The deck notes it was replaced from 1 July 2026, with a 125-day guarantee.
Calling targeting always more efficient. It cuts leakage but raises exclusion errors.
Ignoring political economy. The deck calls the gap a political economy gap.
Seeing UBI as a simple swap. Replacing in-kind services with cash may leave poor households worse off.

recall.q: What happened to India's top marginal tax rate?
recall.a: It fell from 97.5% in the 1970s to 30% now.

recall.q: What are MGNREGS's documented effects?
recall.a: Higher rural wages, lower poverty in lean seasons, less distress migration, durable assets and narrower gender wage gaps.

recall.q: What are the main limits of reservations?
recall.a: They reach only about 10% of the workforce, upper layers capture benefits, certificate disputes arise and private sector compliance is voluntary.

recall.q: What is missing from India's response?
recall.a: A wealth and inheritance tax, private anti-discrimination enforcement, portable protection, an urban guarantee and land reform enforcement.

recall.q: What did the Oxfam tax proposal suggest?
recall.a: A 2% tax on wealth above Rs 10 crore could yield Rs 1.37 lakh crore a year.

sections.title: Inequality and Development Practice
sections.big_idea: Programmes reach the less excluded by default. **Design, measure and organise for the most excluded.**
in_plain_words: Targeting is an equity decision. Targeted programmes cost less per beneficiary but exclude legitimate users and carry stigma, while universal ones cover more but include the non-poor. Proxy tests and community lists each have errors, and social audits help control elite capture. Within any poor group a hierarchy of exclusion runs from poor women to Dalit women to remote areas to disability.

Measurement and accountability follow the same logic. Equity MEL disaggregates by gender, caste, religion, geography and disability, tracks concentration coefficients and adds qualitative work. Downward accountability comes through social audits, RTI and grievance redress. **Theories of change** for inequality work fall into asset building, rights and collective action.

key_terms.meaning: Scoring poverty from observable assets.
-1 means benefits go to the poorest, +1 to the richest.
Public reading of programme records by the community.
Local power holders directing benefits to their networks.
Asset transfer plus income support and inclusion for the extreme poor.
Groups linked from village to district level.

worked_example.title: A quota inside a programme
worked_example.setup: MGNREGS requires one-third of workers to be women. Apply the rule to an illustrative worksite of 120 workers.
steps: One-third of 120 is 120 ÷ 3 = 40.
At least 40 workers must be women.
If a site has only 25 women, it falls short by 40 − 25 = 15.
The quota forces targeting toward a group that self-selection would miss.
worked_example.answer: At least 40 of the 120 must be women, so 25 leaves a shortfall of 15.

mistakes: Reporting aggregate beneficiaries. The slide says averages can improve while the most excluded group gets worse.
Trusting community targeting without accountability. Elite capture can steer benefits to the powerful.
Counting complaints as grievance redress. A portal that only records complaints is not enough.
Funding only service delivery. The slide credits movements for the largest gains against inequality.

recall.q: What does a concentration coefficient of 0 mean?
recall.a: Benefits are distributed in proportion to the population.

recall.q: Which model is the example of effective social audits?
recall.a: Andhra Pradesh.

recall.q: What did the Right to Food Campaign secure?
recall.a: The National Food Security Act (2013), giving 67% of the population an enforceable entitlement.

recall.q: What are the three theories of change?
recall.a: Asset-building, rights-based and collective action.

recall.q: Why does FCRA 2020 matter for inequality work?
recall.a: It bans sub-granting, requires separate accounts and widens government discretion to cancel registrations.

sections.title: Further Reading & Resources
sections.big_idea: Match each source to its question. **Know what a dataset can see**, then state the measure and the data you used.
in_plain_words: This section gives you a reading list, a data guide, a glossary and a checklist. The core texts split into global works (Piketty, Milanovic, Atkinson, Wilkinson and Pickett) and India works (Chancel and Piketty, Drèze and Sen, Ambedkar, Deshpande, Sachar). The data table links each platform to its use.

The data-visualisation slides give three charts to read: the V-shaped top 10% income share, the wealth Lorenz curve and the cross-country top 1% comparison, plus the consumption Gini trajectory. The checklist turns the course into six questions and six mistakes. **The long view** is generational work: sustained redistribution, rights and representation.

diagram.caption: a short route from question to claim

key_terms.meaning: World Inequality Database: top income and wealth shares.
Distributional National Accounts combining surveys, tax and accounts.
Socio-Economic and Caste Census asset data.
World Bank poverty and inequality survey data.
Inequality-adjusted Human Development Index.
Shows whether benefits flow to rich or poor.

worked_example.title: Choose the source and size a gap
worked_example.setup: A colleague asks three questions. Choose the source from the deck's data table, then check one gap.
steps: Consumption by rural and urban households: HCES.
The gender wage gap and formal share: PLFS.
Child stunting by caste and quintile: NFHS.
The deck puts the income Gini near 0.50 and the consumption Gini at 0.35.
The gap is 0.50 − 0.35 = 0.15, the top of the 0.10 to 0.15 range.
worked_example.answer: HCES, PLFS and NFHS, and a Gini gap of 0.15 between income and consumption.

mistakes: Citing a source without its limit. Every dataset in the table has a stated limitation.
Using the consumption Gini alone. It understates income and wealth inequality.
Treating aggregate poverty reduction as evidence of falling inequality. They are related but separate.
Calling income support inequality work when it helps only the moderately poor. The deck calls that poverty work.

recall.q: Which source gives top income shares for 100+ countries?
recall.a: WID.world, using DINA methodology.

recall.q: Which survey gives wage distribution and the gender wage gap?
recall.a: PLFS (NSO).

recall.q: What does the top 10% income share do over 1922 to 2022?
recall.a: It falls from about 50% to about 30% by 1980, then climbs back to about 57%.

recall.q: What are the three theories of change in the checklist?
recall.a: Asset-building, rights assertion and collective action, alongside income support.

recall.q: What is the practitioner's north star?
recall.a: Reduce the distance between the most marginalised and the median.

notes.2: This slide is the map. Twelve sections run from why inequality matters, through measurement and India's own story, to policy and practice. Read them in order the first time, then use the **slide ranges** shown here to jump back to the section you need.
notes.4: Two questions sit under the whole deck: what kind of inequality do you mean, and what is distribution for? Outcome inequality is where people end up, opportunity inequality is the unequal chances on the way. Whether India's growth was good enough **depends on which one you weight**, and over what time horizon.
notes.5: Five channels carry the damage: growth, poverty reduction, health, democracy and mobility. Learn them as one list, because an argument for caring about inequality can run through any of them. The India paragraph sets your task: find **which channels matter for your own programme** and what can be done.
notes.6: Vertical inequality ranks individuals from bottom to top. Horizontal inequality compares groups such as castes, communities and regions. A policy can narrow the first and leave the second untouched, so **check both**. Notice too that India's official Gini rests on consumption data, which understates income inequality.
notes.7: Poverty is a fixed line, and inequality is the distance between people. Either can move without the other. That is the India paradox: absolute poverty fell from roughly 45% to 22% while the top 1% took a growing share. **Say which problem your programme targets** before you claim success.
notes.8: Four theories of justice sit behind most disagreements about inequality: utilitarian, Rawlsian, libertarian and capabilities. Tie each to one idea: the size of the pie, the worst-off person, free exchange, and what people can do and be. When a debate stalls, **ask which theory each side is using**.
notes.9: Piketty's r > g says that when capital earns more than the economy grows, wealth concentrates. Below it sit four cases: one for inequality (incentives) and three against (demand, human capital, political capture). **Trickle-down failed the test** in the 18-country study cited here, so you can answer the incentive argument with evidence.
notes.10: Use this as your revision card for the section: five findings on the left, four lessons for practitioners on the right. The closing paragraph asks the question to carry forward: is inequality **a cause, a consequence or a mediator** of the problem your programme addresses? Write your answer before you move on.
notes.12: Picture the Lorenz curve bowing below the diagonal. The more it bows, the higher the Gini, which runs from 0 to 1. Then read the four limits, especially the last: **a consumption-based Gini for India sits 0.10 to 0.15 points below the income-based figure**.
notes.13: Shares are easier to explain than a Gini. The slide gives the top 1% at about 22.6%, the top 10% at about 57%, the middle 40% at about 28% and the bottom 50% at about 15%. **Half the country earns less than the top 1% alone.** Cite WID.world whenever you use these.
notes.14: The Palma ratio compares the top 10% with the bottom 40%, so it reacts to the extremes. India's top 10% hold 57% and the bottom 50% hold 15%, a ratio of 3.8, so the Palma ratio is higher. The Theil index splits inequality into within-group and between-group parts. **Pick the measure that fits your decision.**
notes.15: Income can hide deprivation. The MPI counts overlapping shortfalls in health, education and living standards, and a household is poor if deprived in at least 33% of weighted indicators. Remember the contrast: **Bihar above 30% poor, Kerala under 5%**. Targeting on income alone misses people.
notes.16: Each data source sees a different part of the distribution. Surveys miss top incomes, tax returns cover only taxpayers, PLFS misses capital income, and WID.world imputes heavily. Use the table as a lookup, and **ask what each source cannot see** before you quote a figure from it.
notes.17: Wealth is more concentrated than income. The top 1% holds about 40% of India's wealth and the bottom 50% about 6%, with the top 10% near 65% (World Inequality Lab, 2022-23). Land adds a Gini of about 0.74, and women own about 14% of land. **Estate duty was abolished in 1985**, so inheritance goes untaxed.
notes.18: Treat this table as a menu. Each measure answers a different question: Gini for trends, shares for politics, Palma for advocacy, MPI for targeting, wealth Gini for land reform, Theil for regional against individual patterns. The slide ends with a rule: **state which measure you use and why**.
notes.20: Income is a flow and wealth is a stock. Wealth earns income by itself and compounds, so taxing income changes little when wealth is the source of power. The slide's evidence: equities returned 15 to 18% a year over 20 years while GDP grew 6 to 7%. **Ownership outpaced work.**
notes.21: Capital income sits at the top. Equity ownership, real estate and family-controlled corporate groups each concentrate it, and the top 10% of investors hold over 90% of equity value. The two boxes give the scale: **205 billionaires, and only 0.07% of Indians paying income tax above Rs 10L**.
notes.22: When r > g, family background matters more with each generation. India had an estate duty from 1953 to 1985 and none since. The HUF lets family wealth be held collectively with separate tax treatment. **The law gives daughters equal shares and practice often falls short**, so the gap repeats.
notes.23: Financialisation means finance grows in weight and returns to owning assets beat returns to work. Mutual fund AUM passed Rs 50 lakh crore in 2024, yet 90% of households held no meaningful financial assets. UPI gave payments access; **wealth needs savings and investment access**, which the poorest still lack.
notes.24: For rural India land is the asset that matters: income, collateral and village power. The numbers to keep are a land Gini of 0.74 and 60% of rural Dalit households landless or near-landless. Zamindari abolition worked, **ceiling laws were evaded through benami transfers**, and the Forest Rights Act is only partly applied.
notes.25: India has no general wealth tax and no inheritance tax, and capital gains are taxed below the top labour rate. The wealth tax ran from 1957 to 2015 and was dropped for raising about Rs 1,000 crore a year. Critics call that a design failure. **Read the Oxfam sum as an illustration** of what redistribution could buy.
notes.26: Revision card for the section: five findings on the left, four implications for practice on the right. The closing paragraph gives the direction of travel. **The next phase of reduction has to address wealth as well as income**, which the slide calls politically harder and structurally more important.
notes.28: Milanovic's elephant curve covers 1988 to 2008. The global bottom and middle gained, mostly Asian workers. The 75th to 85th percentile, rich-country working and middle classes, stagnated, and the top 1% gained enormously. **Between-country inequality fell while within-country inequality rose**, so your place in the distribution set your experience.
notes.29: COVID accelerated trends already under way. The ten richest men's wealth rose from $700 billion to $1.5 trillion while 97M people fell into extreme poverty. India's recovery was **K-shaped**: capital and formal salaries rebounded, informal wages lagged. School closures reached 247 million children, and that loss will last decades.
notes.30: China is the comparison case. Its Gini rose from about 0.28 in 1981 to a peak near 0.49 around 2008, and growth still lifted 800M people out of poverty. The hukou system built an institutional urban-rural gap. **Its wealth concentration rivals India's** despite one-party rule.
notes.31: SDG 10 has six targets, 10.1 to 10.6. Learn 10.1 first: growth of the bottom 40% at a rate above the national average. The slide's warning is that none of the targets happens automatically with growth. **State variation is wide**, with Kerala, Goa and Himachal Pradesh doing well and Bihar, UP and Jharkhand poorly.
notes.32: Skill-biased technological change helps skilled workers and replaces routine tasks, which hollows out the middle of the labour market. For India the slide adds a timing risk: 10 to 12 million new workers a year, and AI that could cut jobs **before manufacturing has absorbed them**.
notes.33: Climate and inequality feed each other. The richest 1% emit more CO₂ than the bottom 50% combined, while the rural poor face drought, flood and heat with the least capacity to adapt. Even climate policy can be regressive: **green taxes need their revenue recycled to low-income households**.
notes.34: Revision card for the section: six global findings and four points for Indian practitioners. Pick out the line that links them, that the informal sector carries the risk from **COVID, automation and climate** at once. Then ask which structural force sits nearest your own programme.
notes.36: India's story starts with colonial rule: deindustrialisation, zamindari landlords and weak institutions. Then came the Nehru period, 1950 to 1980, when high tax rates, nationalisation and the Licence Raj helped push the top 1% share down to about 6%. **That 1980 trough is the baseline** for everything after.
notes.37: After 1991 growth ran at about 5 to 6% a year, and the top 1% share went from 6% in 1981 to 22.6% in 2022. Three channels explain it: a skill premium, an explosion of capital income and unequal access to education. **The poor gained absolutely and lost share**, so both facts hold.
notes.38: Urban households consume about 70% more than rural ones, a ratio of 1.7 times in monthly per capita consumption. Rural India is still large, 69% on the 2011 Census, yet gets less income and fewer services. **Rural wages stagnated after the MGNREGS expansion**, so young workers meet few formal jobs.
notes.39: Goa and Bihar mark the ends of the regional range. Theory predicts convergence, but the record since 1991 shows divergence, so something structural blocks it. Two responses appear: **Finance Commission transfers**, which southern states dispute, and the Aspirational Districts Programme covering 112 districts.
notes.40: Informality covers about 90% of the workforce and carries a formal wage premium of 2 to 3 times. The slide gives five reasons it persists, from costly formal hiring to weak enforcement, plus gig work that is informal by default. **EPFO membership roughly doubled, yet most workers still lack social protection.**
notes.41: Read HCES 2022-23 with both columns open. It shows consumption growth in every quintile and a Gini of about 0.35. The critics say methods changed, top incomes are missed and the survey sits far below national accounts. **Use HCES for poverty and rural-urban gaps, and WID.world for the top.**
notes.42: The billionaire numbers: 9 in 2000, 46 in 2010 and 205 in 2025, with about $941B combined. The Adani example shows wealth built in sectors that depend on government concessions, which the slide calls crony capitalism. Media ownership extends the pattern. **Ask how a fortune relates to a licence or contract.**
notes.43: Wage inequality in the PLFS: a median casual wage of about Rs 11,000 a month against about Rs 25,000 for regular workers, more than double. Women earn 75 to 80% of male wages. Platform workers add a new layer, classed as partners and **often paid below minimum wage**.
notes.44: Use the table as your reference card for India's inequality: top 1% at about 22.6%, consumption Gini about 0.35, land Gini about 0.74, informal share about 90%. Then read the five structural points. The headline is that **inequality here is structural**, rooted in informality, land, caste and regional divergence.
notes.46: Caste is the main horizontal axis. SC poverty is 27% and rural ST poverty 45%, with SC poverty two to three times the upper-caste rate. Audit studies add the present-day mechanism: Thorat and Attewell found fewer positive responses for **Dalit and Muslim names**, while Banerjee and colleagues found a gap only in call centre jobs. History and current discrimination both operate.
notes.47: Reservations are quotas: 15% SC, 7.5% ST, 27% OBC and 10% EWS in central jobs and education, plus 33% of panchayat seats for women. They built a public-sector middle class. The five limits matter as much: **they reach only the formal 10% of the workforce**.
notes.48: Female labour force participation on this slide is 41.7% (PLFS 2023-24), up from 23.3% in 2017-18. Women also earn 75 to 80% of male wages and spend about 5 hours a day on unpaid domestic work. **Unpaid care limits paid work** whatever the market demand.
notes.49: The Sachar Committee found Muslims, 14% of the population, comparable to or in some dimensions worse off than Scheduled Castes. Later work finds partial convergence and continuing gaps. The last paragraph introduces **intersectionality**: disadvantages compound, so a Dalit Muslim woman faces more than any single label shows.
notes.50: Disability raises costs and lowers participation: work participation is about 36% against 48% overall. The RPWD Act 2016 lists 21 categories and reserves 4% of government jobs, but fewer than half of reserved posts are filled. **Build accessibility in from the start**, and track disability status in your MEL.
notes.51: Intersectionality means disadvantages compound. The slide's two cases are Dalit women and Adivasi girls, who face the worst nutrition, delivery, violence and dropout outcomes. For MEL the instruction is practical: **disaggregate by gender and caste together**, because averages hide the group that is falling behind.
notes.52: Revision card for horizontal inequality: six findings, then four design rules. Pick out the rule that changes your data sheet: disaggregate by at least gender, caste category and religion. The closing warning is that **targeting the poor is never neutral**, because social identity shapes who gets reached.
notes.54: NFHS-5 gives the caste and quintile picture, and NFHS-6 now adds national and state fact sheets. Stunting is 29.3% nationally in NFHS-6 against 35.5% in NFHS-5, yet in NFHS-5 it reached 40.3% among SC children and about 50% in the poorest quintile. **Check which survey a figure comes from.**
notes.55: India has near-universal enrolment, but about 55% of rural Grade 5 children cannot read a Grade 2 text, and learning levels differ threefold between the richest and poorest quintiles at age 14 to 16. The two-track school system passes birth circumstances into the labour market. **Use learning levels as your progress metric.**
notes.56: Digital access is a new layer of inequality. About 900M have internet subscriptions, yet male use is roughly twice female use. JAM delivery works at scale, but authentication failures have pushed some of the most vulnerable off rolls. COVID turned the divide into **a learning loss for government school children**.
notes.57: India produces surplus food and ranks 111th on the Global Hunger Index. The slide gives four reasons: affordability, hidden hunger, an imperfect PDS and low dietary diversity. Stunting stands at 29.3% in NFHS-6. **The paradox is a distribution problem**, even though Anganwadis serve 83 million children.
notes.58: The Kerala-UP table anchors the section. Under-5 mortality is 7 in Kerala against 55 to 65 in UP and Bihar, and institutional delivery is 99% against 65 to 75%. Kerala's route was female literacy, public health, land reform and social capital. **Policy choices shaped health beyond what income explains.**
notes.59: Out-of-pocket health spending is regressive because illness costs the poor a larger share of income. 55M people fell below the poverty line in one year, though the out-of-pocket share has dropped from 62.6% to 39%. PM-JAY covers hospitalisation only, while about **60% of spending is outpatient**.
notes.60: Revision card for the section. The findings run from universal enrolment with unequal learning to the digital divide, and the practice rules follow. The closing paragraph names who to look for: **Adivasi and Dalit girls in UP, MP, Bihar and Jharkhand**, where every disadvantage overlaps.
notes.62: The Great Gatsby Curve links higher inequality to lower mobility, using the intergenerational income elasticity (IGE). India is thought to sit at the high-inequality, low-mobility end, especially along caste lines. Denmark, Norway and Sweden show that **policy can build a high-mobility society**.
notes.63: Caste acts as a mobility barrier through discrimination, networks and cultural capital. Hnatkovska, Lahiri and Paul found SC/ST education and income converging between 1983 and 2005. Government jobs under reservation give later generations a **first-mover advantage**, and Ambedkar's graded hierarchy explains why the system persists without constant force.
notes.64: Education should lift people, but quality splits. Mothers' education is the strongest predictor of a child's attainment, and the first generation has the hardest climb. Government schools with high absence give a credential with little market value, and **institutional reputation, as with the IITs, acts as a filter**.
notes.65: Migration moves people toward income while the safety net stays behind. India has 450 to 600M internal migrants, many of them circular. The March 2020 lockdown exposed the lack of portable rations, MGNREGS work and insurance. **The migrant gains income and gives up protection.**
notes.66: Social capital runs through jati networks that pass on jobs, credit and housing, and Dalits and Adivasis have been excluded from many of them. Reservation also inserts people into professional networks, a multiplier for their community. Cities show somewhat higher mobility because **jati-based exclusion is diluted**.
notes.67: Four policies raise mobility: early childhood investment in the first 1000 days, better government schools, portable social protection and anti-discrimination enforcement. The slide calls early childhood the most cost-effective. **One Nation One Ration Card** is the example of portability, still incomplete.
notes.68: Revision card for the section. The evidence list ends with migration as a partial channel, and the practitioner list turns it into actions: improve Anganwadi quality, track first-generation formal employment, build networks, push for portability. The last line says reversal **needs multi-generational investment**.
notes.70: SBTC raises demand and pay for skilled work, replaces routine middle-skill tasks and leaves low-paid service work, which hollows out the labour market. India's IT boom produced its own skill premium. Generative AI could now reach coding, legal research and diagnosis, putting **export earnings** at risk too.
notes.71: Globalisation lowered between-country inequality, yet gains inside India went to the educated, urban and English-speaking. Stolper-Samuelson predicts gains for labour-abundant countries, but India's exports tilted to skilled services. China took the labour-intensive manufacturing path. **India's missing manufacturing middle** concentrated the gains.
notes.72: Countries with similar incomes show very different inequality, and the slide says the difference is policy. Three levers appear: taxes (top rate down from 97.5% to 30%), labour law and informality, and subsidies. **Fertiliser subsidies favour larger farmers**, and DBT is progressive in principle but excludes people without accounts.
notes.73: Financialisation turns market booms into wealth for existing owners. The Nifty rose 5x after 2014, 90% of equity value sits with the top 10% of investors, and the bottom 70% of households have negligible exposure. Add real estate and private equity: **who owned assets before the boom decided who gained**.
notes.74: Discrimination operates now, in hiring, housing and credit. Banerjee and colleagues found lower callbacks for OBC applicants in call centre jobs and no evidence of discrimination in software jobs, so results vary by sector. Dalit and Muslim borrowers face **higher rejection and higher interest**, and land without title cannot be collateral.
notes.75: Three colonial roots: the 1793 Permanent Settlement created hereditary zamindars, India's share of world manufacturing fell from roughly 25% in 1750 to 2% in 1900, and census and legal classification made caste more rigid. History set the starting assets. **Reservation partly answers a problem colonial rule helped create.**
notes.76: Revision card for the section: six causes, each pointing to a different response. Skills training answers technology, anti-discrimination measures answer bias, redistribution answers path dependency. The slide's rule is **no single driver and no single fix**. Match each cause to a response before you draft a programme design.
notes.78: Progressive taxes redistribute directly. India's top rate fell from 97.5% to 30%, capital gains are taxed at 12.5 to 20%, wealth tax ended in 2015 and estate duty in 1985, and GST is somewhat regressive. The tax-to-GDP ratio is about 18 to 19%. The slide calls these measures administratively feasible and **names political resistance as the obstacle**.
notes.79: The table lists five programmes with scale and gap, from PDS at 810M beneficiaries to PM-AWAS. Note the correction on the MGNREGS row: the scheme was replaced from 1 July 2026 and the guarantee rises to 125 days. **Urban informal, migrant, gig and elderly people remain the uncovered groups.**
notes.80: MGNREGS guaranteed 100 days of manual work at minimum wage until 30 June 2026. Evaluations credit it with higher rural wages, less distress migration and durable assets. Budget cuts and late pay weaken it: wages are due within 15 days and often take months. An **urban guarantee** is the proposed extension, piloted in Tamil Nadu.
notes.81: Read the evidence in two columns. For: an SC/ST middle class and better public goods from women's seats. Limits: reach, capture by upper layers within the groups, certificate disputes, and EWS reservation resting on a different basis. **Weigh effectiveness and fairness as two separate questions.**
notes.82: Land redistribution built broad-based assets in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan. India's reform ended zamindari, helped some tenants and set ceilings that were evaded. The slide says existing laws could still do much: ceiling-surplus land, FRA and women's inheritance. **Urban land rules also drive inequality.**
notes.83: UBI means unconditional cash to everyone. The 2016-17 Economic Survey proposed Rs 7,620 per person per year to 75% of the population. Pilots show good spending and no large fall in work. Critics cite a cost of 5 to 7% of GDP, loss of in-kind services and cash reaching men. **No national UBI exists.**
notes.84: Revision card for the whole section: five supported measures and five gaps. Read the final paragraph last. It names the problem as a political economy gap, because concentrated wealth buys concentrated influence. It follows that **building coalitions matters as much as designing the right policy**.
notes.86: Targeting is an equity decision. Targeted programmes cost less per beneficiary but miss eligible people and carry stigma, while universal ones cover more. Proxy means tests use assets, and community lists use local knowledge but invite elite capture. **Pair community targeting with social audits.**
notes.87: Equity MEL asks who benefits as well as how much. Disaggregate by gender, caste, religion, geography and disability. The concentration coefficient runs from -1 (all benefits to the poorest) to +1 (all to the richest), with 0 proportional. Add qualitative methods, since **the excluded are least visible in data**.
notes.88: Accountability usually runs upward to funders. Downward tools come from social audits (Andhra Pradesh is the model), RTI and working grievance redress. A portal that only records complaints is not enough. **Ask whether anyone acts on a complaint** before you call a mechanism functional.
notes.89: Civil society won the National Food Security Act and MGNREGS through organised campaigns. FCRA 2020 limits foreign-funded NGOs, including a ban on sub-granting. The slide separates NGOs, which deliver services, from social movements, which mobilise, and says **the largest gains came from movements**. Decide which role you are playing.
notes.90: Standard targeting reaches the less-excluded poor. Within any poor group the exclusion hierarchy runs from poor women to Dalit women, to remote areas, to disability. Three fixes appear: mobilisers from the same community, federated organising (SEWA, MKSS) and **internal quotas**, like one-third women in MGNREGS.
notes.91: Three theories of change for inequality work. Asset building transfers land, housing, savings or livestock, as in the graduation approach. The rights-based version builds legal literacy and enforcement. The collective action version builds organised power and **has the strongest evidence but is hardest to fund**. Name yours.
notes.92: Revision card for practice. Design points: active targeting, intersectional reach, the universal versus targeted trade-off, asset transfer, collective action. MEL points: disaggregation, concentration, social audits, qualitative methods. The closing question to ask: **is the programme reducing inequality, or only poverty among the moderately poor?**
notes.94: A reading list in two blocks. Global: Piketty, Milanovic, Atkinson, Wilkinson and Pickett, plus the World Inequality Report 2022. India: Chancel and Piketty, Drèze and Sen, Ambedkar, Deshpande and the Sachar report. **Ambedkar's Annihilation of Caste** is free online and a good place to begin the caste argument.
notes.95: The table pairs each data platform with what it gives. Global: WID.world, PovcalNet, LIS, UNDP and OPHI. India: HCES, PLFS, NFHS, SECC and Devdatalab. Match the source to the question: **consumption from HCES, wages from PLFS, health gaps from NFHS** and top shares from WID.world.
notes.96: The glossary holds twenty terms in two columns. Learn them in pairs: Gini and Palma, vertical and horizontal, MPI and IHDI, financialisation and crony capitalism. Cover the right column and **say each definition aloud** before you check. These words return in every later reading on this subject.
notes.97: This slide points to three flagship courses: Development Economics, MEL Essentials and Gender Studies. Use them for the economic framework, for equity-focused evaluation design and for gender inequality. The note at the foot lists other 101 decks. **All are free**, so share them with colleagues.
notes.98: Read the chart as a V. The top 10% share was around 50% before Independence, about 30% at the 1980 trough, and about 57% now. **It has climbed back above its pre-Independence level.** The slide adds that the U-shape is more pronounced for the top 1%.
notes.99: This Lorenz curve is for wealth: the bottom 50% hold about 6% and the top 1% about 40%, giving an implied Gini of about 0.82 against 0.36 for income. **Wealth is the harder problem and income the visible symptom.** Quote the source and year with the figure.
notes.100: Use the checklist before you design anything. Six questions cover your baseline, horizontal axes, reach to the bottom quintile, disaggregation, theory of change and concentration of benefits. Then come six mistakes to avoid. The north star: **does the programme reduce the distance between the most marginalised and the median?**
notes.101: The final word says every development programme works inside inequality. Five conditions make a difference, from naming the inequality you work on to supporting communities' collective power. The closing paragraph sets the time scale: **generational work**, sustained over decades. Write down one action you will take.
notes.102: Top 1% shares across countries: India and South Africa above 21%, Sweden about 12%, and China roughly half the Indian figure. The chart also shows speed, with India rising from about 6% in 1980 to over 21% today. That rise is recent, so **recent causes deserve attention** alongside colonial history.
notes.103: The consumption Gini stayed around 0.32 to 0.33 through the 1990s, then rose with liberalisation. The income Gini is about 0.50 and rose more sharply. The gap reflects **savings behaviour of the rich and survey measurement gaps**. Always say which Gini you are quoting.
